en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Jewel Net, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling at the crossroads by the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
In the vihāra, he was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—sixty thousand bhikṣus who were all arhats;

and thirty billion bodhisattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha). Among them were Maitreya Bodhisattva and others who were bound by two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, eighteen births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, and a hundred births; to speak briefly, up to those who would attain buddhahood after a thousand births.

There were nine billion assemblies of devas: devas of the desire realm, devas of the form realm, the Four Great Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, Susīma, Candraprabha, Sūryaprabha, Jayottama, and Nandika; these sons of gods and other devas numbered nine hundred and ninety million.

Also present were the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Śaṅkha, the Dragon King Vāsuki, the Dragon King Mānasa, the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Upananda, the Dragon King Manasvin, and the Dragon King Mahāpramoda.
Furthermore, the Asura King Kāla and all his asura subjects came to the assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down in their respective sections.
At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, General Siṃha had a son named Anantabala.

This Anantabala had a young son, a noble youth named Ratnajāla, who had already made offerings to hundreds of thousands of countless Buddhas, serving as a great torch for the Dharma throughout immeasurable ages. He was then eight years old.
At that time, as he was asleep, he saw in a dream a deva from Tuṣita Heaven descending from the celestial palace, proclaiming a fragrant sound and praising him with these verses:
“The Buddha’s body is present now to guide sentient beings; Its light shines brilliantly throughout the three thousandfold world-system.
His countenance is exquisite and wondrous, never tiring to behold; His body is the color of purple gold, the gathering of a hundred blessings.”
Even if the light of many moons were multiplied by hundreds of millions, it could not compare to the brilliance of the Sage’s wisdom and countenance;
his palace manifests light in the tens of billions, causing this lunar palace to pervade the eastern quarter.
Just as it is in the south, so too it is in the west; palaces were likewise constructed in the north.
Thus these halls illuminate billions [of worlds], their number equal to the sands of the Ganges.
In the pores of the peerless World-Protector, The radiance he emits shines with majestic brilliance;
From each and every mark and excellence of the Sage, A brilliant light issues forth, illuminating the infinite.
The majestic power exerted by each and every Guide, used to transform and enlighten all sentient beings, exceeds even the number of rivers and streams;
he is universally able to manifest and proclaim these thirty-six [qualities].
Thereupon, the youth Ratnajāla, awakening from his night dream, addressed his father, saying:
"Last night, various devas and humans descended from the Tuṣita Palace and spoke to one another in verse, singing praises to extol the Buddha’s merits."
"Now I wish to seek him out and, having seen him, take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Truly Real One.
Thereupon, the youth Ratnajāla praised him with a verse:
"O Excellent Guide who awakens sentient beings, O Father of the World whose will is vast and free from thought, I take refuge in you, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
Great Being, you should know that making offerings to the Buddha is meritorious; the appearance of a Guide in the world is exceedingly rare.
Like the auspicious *utpala* flower, which is difficult to encounter, its color is brilliant and its texture soft and exquisite;
its fragrance spreads far without diminishing—such a venerable flower is hard to find.
Today, with my body, I address the Great Being; may you grant me your gift with a heart of joy, following the protection of the world and the teaching of the Radiant One.
One should always pay respectful homage to him, who manifests the wisdom of the ultimate truth.
With a heart full of joy, he immediately addressed the youth Li-che and General Siṃha:
"To make offerings to the Great Sage, young man, I shall go; I shall simply follow your command!
If you plant these six hundred million [seeds], cultivate the practice of diligence, and make offerings to the Guide, you shall reverently take refuge in the Lion of the Śākyas."
The most supreme and powerful ones all followed the Lord of Devas; his eyes were a thousand.
Furthermore, the Brahmā King, sovereign in his exalted station, and the sons of the celestial Māra, together with hundreds of millions of *nayuta* of devaputras.
All were filled with joy as they traveled through Vaiśālī.
Numbering in the hundreds of millions, they possessed the color of refined gold like the bright moon;
adorned with the seven treasures, they were most majestic and sublime, each arranged in its own distinct division.
Their number is in the billions;
the couches are all likewise arranged on the right side, with banners and streamers standing tall, providing constant joy and delight.
Perfectly endowed with the subtle and wondrous, his banner is transcendent and supreme;
there are billions of extraordinary banners and streamers, each positioned to his left and right.
Supremely excellent in all its fine qualities, like a bright moon-jewel, it stands out preeminent and pervades everywhere;
each individual jewel is worth billions, and they hang there in ornamental array.
Upon the various banners and streamers, they were firmly erected; the supreme Dharma is exceedingly lofty, and its streamers and tassels are interlaced with purple and gold.
The banners were thus, never separated from the golden [trees].
All the trees were fully filled with billions of thousands; the various seats were peaceful and secure, arranged in rows behind them.
These various seats were firm and sublime; their arrangement was stable and secure, like the threshold of a gate.
Upon the couches and beds, jeweled canopies shone brilliantly, and banners of purple-gold hue hung all around.
Mother-of-pearl in its raw state, as well as agate; the treasures of A-vén, along with pearls;
and that red sandalwood—various kinds of jewels, each one placed before him, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, arranged in intersecting paths all around.
The precious canopy was adorned and fashioned from exquisite gold; it was perfected with crystal, lapis lazuli,
white silver as rare as treasure, musaragalva, and agate.
Upon the ground, each and every one was arranged; each precious vase reached a total of hundreds of thousands.
Incense was burned within them as an offering, presented to the Teacher whose fame is heard afar.
In the space above, with purple-gold, they fashioned jeweled cords;
each individual jeweled cord was most subtle and exquisite, connecting the various jeweled banners,
numbering in the billions.
Calculating those jeweled necklaces, they number in the billions and tens of millions; each one is made of purple-gold, strung together with cords.
Those who come to behold them find them exceedingly beautiful—the people of all the kingdoms, including those of the city of Vaiśālī.
Ascending from below for a height of forty-nine chi,
the city of Vaiśālī was entirely covered with garments and perfumed with red sandalwood incense.
Each offered their robes, pearls, gems, and necklaces, interspersed with purple gold,
numbering seventy trillion;
there were a thousand kinds of bells, all placed at their sides, and seventy trillion incense burners arranged in rows.
Having used these to make offerings to the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, such was the great adornment he prepared.
Then the youth Ratnajāla, with a joyful heart, addressed his parents regarding what had been arranged in the kingdom:
"I went to visit the Buddha, wishing to invite the Most Holy One.
Immediately upon emerging from that city gate, I proceeded to where the Most Victorious,
Great Sage was, prostrated at his feet, and took refuge in the Ocean of Virtue."
The youth then withdrew and stood to one side.
Thereupon, the youth Ratnajālin departed from the great city of Vaiśālī and proceeded to where the Buddha was.
With reverent solemnity and respectful demeanor, he prostrated himself at his feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, taught the Dharma according to what was appropriate for the occasion and what he ought to understand, whereupon [the disciple] rejoiced with great delight.

When the youth Ratnajāla saw the Buddha encouraging and transforming him by preaching the Dharma, he was filled with even greater joy. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with a serene and pleasant countenance, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One will look upon me with compassion and accept my invitation for tomorrow, together with the assembly of noble ones.”
The Buddha, having accepted the invitation, remained silent in response, thereby granting his consent to the youth.
At that time, the Buddha felt compassion for Ratnajāla;
seeing the Buddha’s silence, Ratnajāla rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid his respects, and departed.

The youth Ratnajāla, together with Śakra Devendra, the celestial king Brahmajāla, and the son of heaven Susīma, entered the city of Vaiśālī. They provided meals of a hundred flavors and offered various kinds of exquisite delicacies. Then, during the night, they prepared the seating arrangements and adorned the city of Vaiśālī, hanging up banners and streamers, scattering flowers, and burning incense.
Having completed the preparations, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined, he addressed the Buddha:
"O Great Sage, out of compassion for me, please accept that the time has come and the meal is prepared; it is as you deem appropriate."

Then, at dawn on the following day, the Buddha donned his robes and took up his alms bowl; accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of holy beings, he ascended into the air to a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi*, walking with supernormal power as he desired to enter the city of Vaiśālī.

Just as he was about to enter the city, the Tathāgata caused the trichiliocosm—the world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds—to tremble six times in succession, manifesting eighteen kinds of countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of miraculous transformations.

Upon arriving at Vaiśālī, an infinite number of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas all came forth, raining down celestial flowers—blue lotuses, red, yellow, and white varieties, as well as the *manojñā* (mind-pleasing) flowers of the devas, honey-scented incense, powdered incense, and blended perfumes. Carrying bright moon pearls mixed with purple-gold and various rare, wondrous seven-jeweled celestial blossoms, they scattered them over the Buddha while singing praises in unison. They played an infinite number of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of musical instruments to delight the Buddha; the thunderous sound from the sky was heard throughout the ten directions, and celestial sandalwood rained down, with various precious necklaces adorning everything above and below.

The blind regain their sight, the deaf regain their hearing, the mute are able to speak, the sick are healed, the lame are able to walk, the insane regain their composure, the distracted attain concentration, the hunchbacked are straightened, and for those afflicted by poison, the venom is entirely neutralized.

The *konghou* lute played music spontaneously without being struck; the pearl rings on the women’s arms jingled as they brushed against one another; and birds and beasts cried out in mournful harmony. The multitude gathered to witness this, all of whom were filled with joy and wonder.

At that time, as soon as the World-Honored One had entered the city, the devas held various precious canopies above and below him in the air. The Buddha then proceeded to the house of the youth Ratnajāla and sat down before it; he was accompanied by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, all of whom sat there in their respective order.

When the youth Ratnajāla saw that the Buddha’s disciples were already seated, he personally served a hundred kinds of food and various flavors of extraordinary delicacies, making offerings to the World-Honored One and the fourfold assembly of noble disciples with equal and no distinction.

When the meal was finished and the water for washing had been served, he took three Dharma robes, each worth countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis, and offered them to the Great Sage, the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣuṇīs; they likewise all received three sets of Dharma robes, the value of which was equal to that given to the Buddha, without any difference.
Each of the laymen and laywomen of pure faith was presented with a complete set of robes. Why was this so?
It was because they had all been transformed by the holy grace of the World-Honored One, which caused it to be thus.

After the youth Ratnajāla had finished making offerings to the Buddha, he set aside his own hunger and, having settled himself, took a separate seat before the Buddha. Sitting to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if you would grant me leave, I shall venture to speak."
The Buddha told Ratnajālin: "Ask whatever you wish.
For all those who have doubts, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, shall untie the net of their entanglements and cause their minds to be at ease."
The youth asked the Buddha:
"Indeed, Great Sage! Is it the case that there are Buddhas who, having practiced their vows in past worlds, have now brought them to fulfillment in the present?"

Those sons and daughters of noble family who study the bodhisattva path and train in the bodhisattva vehicle, upon hearing his name, will attain clarity and understanding in their hearts and harbor no doubts; they shall become non-retrogressive and shall surely attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.

His physical form was upright and his complexion was peerless; his wealth was inexhaustible, his precepts were without flaw, and he was fully endowed with wisdom. Possessing the knowledge of past lives, he harbored no greed or envy and was free from all delusive thoughts. Wherever he was, he was always peaceful and harmonious, taking the various bodhisattvas as his retinue and distancing himself from all the assembly of śrāvakas, thereby receiving and accepting the merits of what was taught.

Incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, hold him in high esteem and love; he satisfies the long-standing hunger and emptiness of sentient beings; he startles all Māras so that they all come to take refuge in him; he cultivates and adorns the lands of the Buddhas; he clears away the cataracts and defilements of the minds of sentient beings; and he proclaims the pure and white Dharma. All celestial deities and spirits together protect him, and all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas keep him in mind. Established by the Tathāgatas, the Truly Realized Ones, he never strays from the presence of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. He fully masters all the practices of a Bodhisattva and is complete in the eighty-four thousand varieties of activities. His ultimate voice, like that of Brahmā, penetrates the entire Buddha-realm; there is none who does not hear it, and all receive his command.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Ratnajāla: "Excellent! Excellent!"

The eloquence with which you have questioned is most subtle and refined; it brings great cause for concern yet also great peace and security. Out of compassion for the devas and the people of the ten directions, you are able to interrogate the Tathāgata on such a profound meaning!
Listen attentively, young man!
Reflect upon it well!
I shall explain it for you, analyzing its meaning.
The youth Ratnajāla and the great assembly received the instruction and listened attentively.
The Buddha said: "O Youth!

You should know that to the east of here, there is a buddha-world named *Vimukta*. Suppose, noble son, there were as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; from the lowest water-base up to the upper realm of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, these fields were filled everywhere with motes of dust.

At that time, there was a man who emerged from there of his own accord; he counted every single dust mote of all those worlds, placing one dust mote only after passing beyond several hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayuta* of Buddha-fields.
The Buddha said, "Young man!

To use this analogy, suppose one were to place a single mote of dust upon each of the buddha-fields enumerated previously, continuing for a vast, remote, infinite, and immeasurable duration beyond all calculation, until even space could no longer contain the number of these motes; and suppose one were then to gradually remove them until they were entirely exhausted—what do you think, young man?"
Could anyone possibly conceive, calculate, weigh, or compute the number of particles moved by that man, or the distance—whether far or near, many or few—at which they were deposited?
He replied: "There is no one capable of knowing it, O God among Gods!

Even if there were someone who wished to analyze, identify, and explain this parable, or to clarify its meaning, they would still be unable to fully comprehend the parable itself; how much less could they know its number?"
The Buddha said to the youth:

“The dust particles moved by that man at each point where they were placed constitute the realms of the Buddhas; from the lower limit of the water’s edge up to the upper limit of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the number of lands filled with such dust is incalculable.”

Then, a second person appeared and took one of those dust motes; having passed as many Buddha-fields as the number of dust motes previously calculated by the first person—traversing several incalculable, immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Buddha-fields—he then placed that dust mote down.
The Buddha said,
“Son of good family! By this analogy,
having traversed the vast and boundless distance to the east, one takes another mote of dust and passes over it as many times as before, then places another mote of dust there.”

By means of such analogies, the distance that person must traverse—where the heavens do not cover it and the earth cannot support it, across incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields—is only then reached upon arriving at the world of Jñānottara.

In that world there is a Buddha named Ratnārciścandramaṇḍala, titled the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who currently resides there.

Sons of good family and daughters of good family who study the Bodhisattva vehicle, upon hearing the name of that Buddha, shall harbor no doubt; for those who believe in the Buddha’s eye of wisdom are worthy to hear his name, and wherever they are born, they shall become universal monarchs (cakravartin).

If one encounters the Buddhas whenever they appear in the world, beholding countless Buddhas, the Most Honorable and Truly Realized Ones, and makes offerings to them all; if one purely cultivates the Brahma-conduct and attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); if one advances and retreats with peerless mastery, possessing sovereign power over *dhāraṇī*; if one attains the vision of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the Equal and Perfectly Awakened Ones; if one abandons birth and death for as many hundreds of millions of kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; if one’s mind is always tranquil and never forgetful; if one constantly resolves upon the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; if one is free from defilement and does not associate with worldly dust; if by attaining sovereignty one’s body is like a linked chain; if dwelling in a single place one is fully endowed with the four requisites; if one’s physical form is like purple-gold, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; if one attains the eightfold voice comparable to that of Brahmā; and if one casts off the eight difficulties and always dwells in leisure and tranquility.
Then, the World-Honored One, having contemplated this meaning, spoke in verse:
“Those who hear the name of the World’s Roar, And harbor no doubt in their hearts,
But firmly believe in the clarity of the Buddha-Dharma, They shall be true benefactors of the multitude.”
Constantly becoming a Wheel-Turning King, he invariably encounters and beholds the Buddhas;
upon meeting them, he immediately makes offerings beyond measure and beyond reckoning.
Ever observing and practicing the holy life, his supernormal powers are peerless.
Holding and turning all dhāraṇīs, they reach the path of all Buddhas;
they constantly behold the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
transcending all births and deaths for many billions of kalpas.
Because he was resolved upon the Buddha-way, his mind never once forgot it;
proclaiming the name of the World-Honored Roarer, he requested the assembly to spread its teaching.
He became a Wheel-Turning Sage King, established in a state of sovereign freedom.
His body is of purple-gold color, and his marks are the thirty-two.
If anyone hears the Buddha’s name, his voice will be like that of Brahmā;
they shall abandon the eight states of adversity and prostrate themselves in fivefold homage.
They do not obstruct the Buddha-way, nor have they ever harbored anger or resentment;
for those who hear the name of the Buddha do not harbor doubt.
If one reveres the name of the Most Victorious One for seven days, morning and night, throughout the entire time, [one shall attain liberation].
That eye attains purity, reaching the vision of immeasurable Buddhas;
without abandoning the fleshly eye, one sees everywhere with clarity,
beholding countless Buddhas like the sands of the Ganges.
The Buddha told the youth:

"If there are bodhisattvas, as well as ordinary persons, who hear the names of those Buddhas and, with diligent and earnest contemplation, take refuge from afar and offer worship to them all, they shall hear everything spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions and behold them all with their own eyes, and they shall all believe and rejoice."

Having in past lives made offerings to countless Buddhas, as soon as they hear the names of these Tathāgatas, they immediately recognize and recall all their former wanderings; they explain the origins and details of their past lives and their respective names, and they perceive the vows they have made and the fundamental dispositions from which the roots of other beings arise.

Having reached the ultimate path of the Buddha, his heart is filled with joy; it is as vast as the rising sun, forever free from the obscuration of dust. What he perceives is infinitely expansive; he has cast aside the eight difficulties and all matters of strife, his mind being harmonious and gentle, always dwelling in tranquility.

If there are those with sincere faith in the Buddha-way, they will remain harmonious and never feel anxious or fearful even when separated from others; even if they committed various transgressions in past lives that would have required them to suffer burning and roasting for kalpas in the evil realms, their myriad calamities will be eliminated upon encountering a mere headache.
Fire cannot bring calamity, nor can wind cause harm; even sovereign rulers and kings cannot inflict injury.

Upon hearing the name of the Tathāgata, one who was previously born blind shall no longer suffer from eye pain or blindness, nor shall they be deaf or mute. Because of hearing the Buddha’s name, one shall not be hunchbacked or lame.

No dragons, ghosts, spirits, asuras, hungry ghosts, or yakṣas—neither humans nor non-humans—could violate or disturb it; no malevolent demons, violent spirits, divine dragons, or terrestrial deities failed to cherish and delight in it.
"If those who uphold the names of the Buddhas possess such merit as this, it is beyond measure or calculation.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"With their eyes they see all the Buddhas, And are all able to make offerings to them."
Upon hearing what was said, they immediately accepted it, and all those people believed and rejoiced.
Regarding the successive lives they had experienced in past existences and the countless Buddhas they had made offerings to,
as soon as they heard the names of those Buddhas, they recognized and remembered them all.
I shall proclaim their original names and titles for the sake of all people.
Furthermore, seeing other sentient beings who are able to bring the Buddha-way to ultimate fulfillment,
they give rise to a heart of joy and cast off all eight difficult conditions.
Having cut away all disputes and litigation, one’s life shall always be tranquil and still.
Even if one is renowned for their faith, as a protector of the world and a true lord of the Dharma,
their mind harbors no fetters, having cast off all matters of clamor and distraction.
Even if one has committed a sin of immediate retribution and must suffer its calamities for many kalpas,
upon encountering a single instance of a headache, all such transgressions shall be forever eradicated.
One will not be harmed by fire, nor will one be caught in the midst of wind.
Having heard the name of the Tathāgata, the king could not inflict harm upon him.
He was never born blind, nor deaf, nor mute;
by honoring the Most Victorious One, his hands and feet remained complete and unimpaired.
Ghosts, spirits, and gandharvas, hungry ghosts and malevolent deities—
if they hear the name of the Tathāgata invoked, human poisons and curses shall not take effect.
Whether they be various mārīs or rākṣasas, or various devas and nāgas, [they shall likewise be subdued].
"By upholding these most supreme names, all shall together love and revere them.
The Buddha again addressed the youth:

"If there should be anyone who hears the name of that Buddha, they will swiftly attain samādhi, resolve all doubts, and remain unattached to sounds and echoes; their resolve shall be such that no toil or merit arises, even across billions of kalpas."
The reason for this is that they have heard the name of the Buddha.

If, upon encountering the name of the Buddha, one is composed and free from doubt, then one will be able to uphold it and transcend countless kalpas; such is the merit of those who believe and rejoice in this Dharma during the final age.

If one hears the name [of the Buddha] after the Guide has entered parinirvāṇa, and skillfully proclaims, upholds, and expounds his Dharma teachings; if one can recite and cherish the sūtras preached by the Honored One among Men; if one cultivates purity to reach the state of honor and prepares for all the practices of the Buddhas; then at the time of death, one’s mind will not be disturbed, and one will immediately behold billions of Buddhas and be able to receive and uphold all the Dharma they preach.

Having already established themselves through self-cultivation to transform and enlighten sentient beings, they do not seek out faults when hearing [the names of others], but transform them all, causing them to abide in the Buddha-way; if such persons should uphold the names of the Buddhas, they are worthy of making offerings to the Great Sages, the Buddhas.
Furthermore, those who believe that my body follows the teachings of the Buddha and constantly take refuge in me shall forever attain liberation and not go to hell.

Those who believe in the Buddha’s wisdom take refuge in my person; those who slander it are the followers of Māra. The World-Honored One saves all such beings wandering through the five destinies, establishing them in the Single Vehicle.
"From a single pore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, can emit as many rays of light as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, thereby delivering sentient beings.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Do not doubt the sounds and phrases; Swiftly you shall attain samādhi."
The flourishing and fulfillment of billions of meritorious deeds are brought about by hearing the names of the Buddhas.
In the future age of the final dharma, those who uphold the Way of this sutra and hear the names of the World-Honored Roar will have no hesitation in their hearts.
Regarding all the Perfectly Awakened Ones who have entered parinirvāṇa,
if one hears the names of these many Teachers as they proclaim the Dharma teachings,
and upholds them with discernment, then one has fully practiced what all Buddhas have expounded.
One is able to attain noble purity, which is appropriate for all the sages.
When the time approaches for the end of one's life, one immediately beholds billions of buddhas and is always able to receive and accept all the teachings spoken by those buddhas.
Having already attained the establishment of practice, they transform billions of sentient beings;
what they have heard is not in vain, as they universally establish the path of all Buddhas.
Thus, they fully uphold and maintain all the teachings of the Buddhas.
Those who believe in my true holy eye, and likewise make offerings to all Buddhas,
taking refuge in the Most Victorious Ones, shall forever cross over the evil realms.
Those who believe in the Buddha’s wisdom follow my teaching.
If one loves the Dharma of the Buddha-way, they follow the teachings of the Great Sage;
if they slander the True Dharma, they are all the retinues of Māra.
As for all the pores on the bodies of sentient beings within the five destinies,
"Saving from peril in such numbers as these, they enter the path of the One Vehicle.
The Buddha told the youth:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, by means of a single pore, manifests light and majestic spiritual power equal to the sands of the Ganges River. If there are those who believe this, they shall behold hundreds of millions of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, within a single lifetime."
If, moreover, one hears this teaching spoken by the Dharma King and does not harbor the net of fetters, one shall likewise attain Buddhahood, just as I do now.

Furthermore, if one follows and expounds this sutra, there will be rare believers in the final age; like the sands of the Ganges, such individuals will pervade the world-systems, and the Buddha-fields they illuminate will be thus inconceivable.

Even if one were to calculate all these numbers and offer treasures filling them as alms to the Tathāgata, yet if one further hears the Buddha’s name with a heart full of joy, they shall attain this inconceivable wisdom.
To repeatedly contemplate the Honored Ones, the Teachers, brings merit and blessings that are beyond measure.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s radiance illuminates the ten directions, and his body is majestic, as if composed of precious jewels.

Furthermore, if one hears the Buddha’s name and harbors no doubt, one will immediately attain the state of non-arising; the breath from one's mouth will be fragrant, and its renown will spread far and wide. To proclaim and uphold the Buddha’s name brings such merit that it is beyond measure.
The Buddha then spoke in verse: "From within a single pore,
the Sage Roaring in the World, with holy majesty and spiritual power,
emanates rays of light, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
If there are those who have faith in this, that the immeasurable light of all Buddhas is realized in a single lifetime, they shall behold billions of Buddhas.
If one hears this sutra, which is praised and extolled by the Dharma Kings, [one shall attain such realization].
If one reflects upon this without doubt, they shall surely attain what I have now attained.
Those who, when the time is right, hear this sutra being preached,
shall thereafter, in the final age, explain it in detail for others.
Like the sands of the Ganges, they praise the grounds upon which the Great Being relies;
with a single radiant light, he illuminates manifold Buddha-fields.
Even if one were to calculate them all together, those Buddha-fields would be inconceivable.
If one were to fill [the world] with purple-polished gold and personally offer it to the World-Protectors,
yet hear the names of the Buddhas and harbor a mind of serene composure—
this would not equal the merit of praising the Buddhas' names; such merit is most limitless.
One who can constantly and repeatedly bring to mind the Truly Realized,
the Perfectly Awakened One, is unable to fully extol or exhaustively calculate his merit.
The light emanating from his body is as brilliantly radiant as a precious gem.
If one hears the names of the Buddhas, one shall not harbor lingering doubts or hesitations.

Upon attaining the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), the breath from one's mouth will be fragrant and sweet, like celestial sandalwood incense; all this arises from proclaiming the names of the Buddhas.
The Buddha said to the youth Ratnajāla:

"Suppose a person were to hear of the light emanating from the pores of the Buddha’s body; its radiance shines afar, enlightening and guiding sentient beings so that their hearts are filled with joy. Wherever they are born, they shall serve the Buddhas, never remaining far from their side, just as Ānanda now comes to serve the Buddha, like a son, a grandson, or a close kinsman."
By practicing the Buddha-way to bring clarity to the world, one brings forth immeasurable joy; the resulting reverence and devotion are beyond measure.
Having beheld the Buddhas, one serves them fully and thereby attains such merit.
Who, upon hearing the name of the Buddha, would not reverently accept it?
Only the retinues of Māra, the deluded, and those outside the Way could fail to believe. O Youth!
Those who, upon seeing the Buddha, immediately take refuge in this sutra and its Dharma, shall find it in the final age.

Holding it in their hands, contemplating it with their minds, and reciting it with their mouths—those who have previously seen the Buddha expound the meaning of this honored sutra and are able to make diligent offerings to it—to such people these sutra scrolls shall belong; they will naturally come into their own hands.
That which the Dharma King has praised and established, through his sincere vows, shall certainly be attained in future generations.

If one were to serve countless Buddhas with a single mind, it would not equal the merit of believing in the essentials of this sutra; such blessings are immeasurable, surpassing offerings made to all Buddhas. One’s appearance will be upright and handsome, courageous and fearless; one’s merits will be extraordinary, wealth incalculable, and the will firm and strong. Adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, one’s auspiciousness will be fully manifested.
The Buddha then spoke these verses:
“If there are those who hear of the pores of the Buddha’s body,
Of his name and his radiant brilliance, They shall be able to guide and transform sentient beings.”
In every place of birth throughout successive lifetimes, may one always serve as an attendant to the Buddhas,
just as Ānanda serves me, hearing the Dharma and immediately receiving and upholding it.
May one be like a son or a kinsman, reverently practicing the path of a bodhisattva.
When one beholds the light of the world, joy is immeasurable.
Having attained the sight of the most supreme flavor, love and reverence are beyond compare;
by fully serving him, one constantly attains the wisdom of the wondrous path.
Who, upon hearing the name of the Guide, would not respectfully receive it?
Only the retinues of Māra and the heretics lack firm faith.
The elder’s son Ratnajāla, upon seeing the Buddha, immediately began to serve and support him.
Thereafter, in the final age, the sutras and the Dharma shall come into their hands.
Having previously heard the Buddha’s exposition, they shall discern this honored scripture;
if one makes offerings and takes refuge, it will naturally fall into their grasp.
What the Dharma King has taught— One should receive this wondrous scroll,
Establish this right aspiration, And in future lives it will be naturally attained.
If one serves with single-minded devotion, Countless Buddhas [will be honored].
Whoever has faith in this sutra, their merit shall surpass that [of the former].
Their countenance will always be upright and handsome; their achievements will be beyond all fear.
Their wealth will be vast and their resolve firm; they will be naturally adorned with the marks and signs of excellence.
The Buddha told the youth:

“If sons of good family or daughters of good family, hearing this sutra now, should encounter this Dharma in the future final age, and uphold, recite, read it, and expound it for others, they will see the turning of the wheel of Dharma by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and make offerings to them all.”

Thereafter, in the final age, they will not doubt the eye of the Way; having heard the names of the countless Buddhas whom their predecessors served, they will believe with deep sincerity and clear vision, protecting the True Dharma and following the teachings of all Buddhas; upon hearing their names, they shall create images of the Buddhas.

Those who are foolish and obscured by darkness, upon hearing the name of the World-Honored One, harbor malice and slander him; for a hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas they shall remain blind and sightless. Those who, throughout incalculable kalpas, incite strife among sentient beings and slander this sutra, their transgression exceeds that of the former; it is for this reason that I speak thus.

Those who encounter this in future generations must not harbor doubts or lack faith in the Buddha's wisdom; they should diligently offer incense, flowers, and blended perfumes with a devoted mind, and present robes as offerings. Those who hear this sutra should be reverent and diligent in this way, remaining peaceful, composed, and orderly.

The youth Ratnajāla presented clothing and food to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, never letting his mind stray from him; after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, various devas and spirits dwelling in the void rained down celestial flowers as an offering to those who hear this sutra and delight in it with faith and joy, their single-mindedness free from hesitation.
The Buddha then spoke in verse: "If,
in the final age of the future, one should hear this sutra,
receive and uphold it, recite it, and explain it to others,"
They made offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, those who turn the wheel of Dharma;
yet in the final age to come, because they will not doubt the Buddha’s teaching,
they shall have served and sustained the World-Protectors throughout countless kalpas of the past.
Furthermore, if there should be someone who hears the names of these Buddhas,
believes in and delights in the True Dharma, follows the teachings of all Buddhas,
and upon hearing this sutra-dharma, creates images of the Buddhas.
Foolish and harboring the darkness of ignorance, they slander this name of the Buddha;
blind and sightless, they shall suffer this calamity for billions of kalpas.
If one were to dwell through incalculable kalpas, causing strife, discord, and separation among people, [the retribution would be the same].
If one were to slander this sutra, their sin would exceed that [of the former];
therefore, for the sake of future generations, I have explained this meaning.
Do not harbor hesitation or doubt regarding the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom.
With various kinds of incense and flowers, mixed perfumes and fine garments,
upon hearing such a sutra scroll, one should reverently make offerings.
Providing peaceful and harmonious food and drink— this was the youth Ratnajāla.
With soft and exquisite offerings, they repeatedly presented them to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the devas and humans let out great sounds of acclaim;
the devas rained down various flowers, scattering them from afar as they heard this sutra.
The Buddha told the youth Ratnajāla:

"This sutra brings great peace and security; it is like a person suffering from a grave illness who encounters a skilled physician to treat their disease, whereby wind, cold, and heat disorders are all cured without exception."
"In this way, when a bodhisattva hears the name of that Buddha, through diligent and earnest application, the diseases of lust, anger, and ignorance are all completely eliminated.

At that time, an immeasurable multitude of devas and humans gathered in the air and rained down sandalwood incense; hundreds of millions of Brahmās and their sons, upon hearing the title of this sutra and the name of the Tathāgata, leaped for joy, and wholesome minds arose within them.
That which he proclaimed with his mouth was this praise of the Unsurpassed:

"In the final age, we shall become bhikṣus; with firm resolve and fearlessness, we shall propagate this sutra throughout the commanderies, kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages, following the Buddha's teachings."
Even if they were a hundred thousand *yojanas* away, one should go to receive their instructions, not regarding the vast distance as an obstacle.
One should invite the devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, and for them expound the meaning of the sūtras to satisfy them with the Dharma.
The devas were filled with joy, scattering flowers from mid-air that fell like rain. Each of them offered praise, saying:

"With a single voice, the Dharma King proclaims throughout the Buddha-fields to manifest the unconditioned and out of compassion for sentient beings; this pervades as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges, and so it is in the ten directions."

The youth Ratnajāla covers all Buddha-fields; if one beholds the Great Hero, there shall be no weariness. When the World-Honored One looks upon them, he explains it for their sake: do not doubt that the Buddha-dharma and the Tathāgata are immeasurable.

The Buddha’s eye is boundless, universally bestowing peace and security; the Buddha’s wisdom is limitless, penetratingly knowing the three periods of time. There is nothing he does not comprehend as the King of all dharmas. He perceives that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of the world lack any solidity or essence, and the same is true of the four great elements (*mahābhūtas*).

Do not cling to sounds, forms, the aggregates of sensation (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), or volitional formations (saṃskāra). One who understands these realizes that there is no essential core. Those who contemplate what the Tathāgata has taught will swiftly attain dhāraṇī and their resolve will not become confused or desolate. All phenomena are fundamentally pure, empty, and devoid of self; they are without expectation and have no peer—such is the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Countless devas, numbering in the billions, dwell in the void;
They rain down sandalwood incense, and billions of Brahmās likewise scatter it."
Having heard this Jewel Net Sūtra, they praise and encourage the Tathāgata;
their hearts are joyful and glad, and their mouths proclaim the unsurpassed meaning.
In the final age to come, I shall become a courageous bhikṣu.
One should go to cities, towns, and villages, and there proclaim this sutra.

One should faithfully follow the Buddha’s teaching; because of the auspiciousness of the Perfectly Awakened One, one shall travel even hundreds of millions of yojanas to disseminate these words of instruction.
I invite all the devas and humans, the nāgas and gandharvas, and all humans and non-humans; I satisfy them with the gift of Dharma.
All devas and humans rejoice, their minds harmonious, joyful, and at peace.
There, they rained down a multitude of flowers, and with one voice they all uttered words of praise.
Throughout all the Buddha-fields, within the realm of the Dharma King—
the Lion of the Śākyas, the Honored One among Men— the light from a single pore shone forth.
The Guide arouses compassion; the World-Honored One once extends his tongue, which covers billions of buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In the ten directions it is likewise so, each illuminating billions of buddha-fields.
The Great Hero then declared:
"The people of the Plow-Cart country, along with their sixty companions, attended upon the World-Honored One there; looking back at them, he spoke these words:"
"Do not harbor doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma; the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
No one can limit the Buddha-eye, which bestows peace upon all beings in harmony.
The Buddha’s wisdom is boundless, flowing universally throughout the three periods of time."
The World-Honored One has nothing he does not penetrate; He fully understands all the sūtras.
That the five aggregates are without solidity Is what the Guide among Men has taught.
Regarding the transformations of the four great elements, One should not become attached to sounds or echoes.
One should understand that within the aggregate of form, In sensation, perception,
volitional formations, and consciousness, There is nothing that possesses any essential reality.
Discerning the five aggregates in this way, One accords with the instruction of the Tathāgata.
One swiftly attains dhāraṇī, with a mind that never forgets.
All phenomena are fundamentally pure; they are void and devoid of self.
Without contention and without conceptual thought—this follows the teaching of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told the youth:

"To the south, at a distance from here equal to the number of atoms mentioned in the previous analogy, multiplied by twice that number, and further surpassing seventy-two billion hundred thousand *nayutas* of incalculable Buddha-fields by a factor of two, there is a world named Variegated Jewel Brocade. There dwells a Buddha named King of Tree-Root Flowers, who currently teaches the Dharma."

If sons of good family or daughters of good family hear the name of that Buddha—Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—and [hear] the Dharma he has expounded, which is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.

"If sons of noble family or daughters of noble family, upon hearing the name of that Buddha, do not harbor doubts or fetters but believe in my Dharma-eye, they shall, in this present life, become fully endowed with supreme virtue and attain five dharmas."
What are these five?
First, to completely eliminate the notion of self, so that in whatever place one is born, one always encounters the era of a Buddha;
second, to attain the supreme power and status of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
Third, to attain the dharma of dhāraṇī and to faithfully uphold and govern the sūtras in hundreds of thousands of ways;
fourth, to accomplish the thirty-two marks of a great man and to fully perfect all practices until the attainment of the Buddha-way;
fifth, to attain the five supernormal powers without any obstruction or hindrance.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are five things by which one attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). What are these five?

First is the power of penetrating vision, by which one sees throughout the ten directions all things coarse or subtle, large or small—beings in training and those beyond training, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, up to the World-Honored One who transcends all multitudes;

second is the power of penetrating hearing, by which one hears the cries of burning and roasting, hunger and thirst, and the afflictions of the trillions of hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, as well as the peace, security, suffering, and joy of the heavens and the world, whether evil or good, and all the sūtras preached by the Buddhas of the ten directions, hearing them all completely;
third is the power of bodily flight, by which one travels through all Buddha-lands like the sun appearing in water, manifesting coming and going yet without any actual wandering.

The fourth is: to be able to know the mental thoughts of all sentient beings—whether they are good or evil, beautiful or ugly, resolute or irresolute, with outflows or without outflows, with mind or without mind, longing for the mundane or delighting in the Way—and to know them all completely;

the fifth is: to know one’s own past lives and to see the events of countless eons of sentient beings, including their births in ancient times, as well as matters of the past, future, and present, such that there is nothing not understood and all is clearly remembered.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Whoever praises the Great Sage among men, And upon hearing this, does not harbor doubt but always understands it clearly,
Such a person will swiftly attain And reach the five supernormal powers."
Revering this honored scripture spoken by the Buddha, with countenance upright and body like purple-gold,
one shall become a sovereign lord, a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
With a body like a hook and chain, one thereby becomes possessed of merit; establishing dignified deportment, one attains mastery.
His blessings flourish and prosper, and he is endowed with a thousand sons—valiant heroes whose prowess is unsurpassed in their stride.
His countenance is exquisite, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence; by virtue of his meritorious deeds, he is like a celestial sovereign.
If he becomes a king, a thousand court ladies attend him; his body is like celestial gold, and his mental nature is supreme.
Beholding this king, one never tires of gazing upon him; whatever deeds he performs, he does not regard them as a burden.
All his ministers and every noble official who comes to see him never grows weary.
Thus accomplished, the foremost in great virtue, to whom the devas come for refuge, his aspirations are difficult to surpass.
The people of the world, as well as the nāga kings, all together establish the boundaries of the realm for the sake of sentient beings;
they are all able to re-establish it in the place of the Buddha-way.
That land shall be most peaceful, abundant, and impartial; you shall become a self-enlightened Buddha for the sake of the world.
All shall come to that place to pay the highest respect; from beginning to end, the Way shall never be neglected.
As for those who possess knowledge, having heard the name of the Buddha, how could they harbor doubt? They love and revere that which is known;
regarding the Dharma as supreme, they spread its majestic radiance and inquire into this honored sutra spoken by the Buddha.
Truly, in previous lives, he received the Dharma from the Buddhas and swiftly attained nirvana, adhering to and practicing the correct path.
Whenever there were Buddhas who guided sentient beings, his conduct was honored and respected, and he was fully endowed with all virtues.
Those who have faith and joy are called "youths"; they are pure, noble, and possess the wealth and enterprise of kings.
These youths are humble and serve the Buddha; those who hear this name will have no doubt whatsoever.
The Buddha told the youth:

"To the west, beyond the distance described in the previous analogy multiplied three times by the number of atoms, and further transcending twelve *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* buddha-fields, there is a world named Supreme Moonlight (*Jyotir-vimala*). There, the Buddha is named King-Creator of Supernatural Powers Radiant Flower Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One; he currently dwells there, preaching the Dharma."

If sons of good family or daughters of good family who study the Bodhisattva vehicle hear the name of that Buddha and, without harboring doubt, believe resolutely in the Way, they will, in whatever place they are born and according to what they themselves proclaim, attain the Samādhi of Radiant Emanation; immediately thereafter, they will successively reach ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various samādhi-doors and enter sixty incalculable assemblies of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various dhāraṇī-doors, such as the Ocean-like Dhāraṇī and the Treasure-Treasury Dhāraṇī, and thereafter they shall not lose these dharmas of meditative concentration.

At the time of his passing, he beheld with his own eyes ten billion nayutas of Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, in each of the ten directions; all the teachings expounded by those Buddhas of the ten directions he was able to receive and uphold without losing the Way of the Dharma. Until he attained the Way of Buddhahood, he transcended the hardships of birth and death for five hundred kalpas. Abiding in this study for not long, he immediately accomplished the unsurpassed, right, and true path, becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Having heard the name of the Honored One among Men, A Sage of Holy Brilliance who protects the world,
One casts off all births and deaths, Fully perfected over five hundred kalpas."
At the time their lives were drawing to a close, each saw ten billion Buddhas;
they immediately bowed their heads in refuge and inquired after and received the Dharma they had heard.
As for the sutras they had listened to, they never forgot them for even a hundred million eons.
Diligently practicing the sublime and honored conduct, they hear the names of all Tathāgatas;
throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, they abide in the jewel-like samādhi.
They give rise to billions of meritorious virtues, all because they have heard the names of the Buddhas.
Reaching sixty billion eons, for an incalculable number of years,
because they honored the name of the Teacher and served him with offerings,
all these courageous ones have followed and cultivated the practice of the Buddha-way.
He transformed countless thousands of people, establishing them in the supreme path;
having thoroughly understood the Buddha-dharma, he never practiced worldly desires.
He illustrated the conduct of sentient beings and established their respective names.
Those who hear this name shall expound it widely to all;
they shall never fall into the eight difficult conditions and shall easily encounter places of quietude.
Having eliminated all perils and calamities, this is what the Buddha now proclaims.
That person shall always be at ease, encountering the world of a subtle and wondrous Buddha.
If the youth possesses understanding and insight as clarified by the Tathāgata,
those who hear his name shall all be illuminated for these sentient beings.
One should immediately use this sutra to proclaim and expound it for others.
Such is the World-Honored Rightly Awakened One; the Protector of the World saves many.
Those who hear this name shall receive it with harmony and open receptivity.
When one explains this to others, they will protect the Buddha-dharma;
those who protect the Buddha-dharma skillfully proclaim the causes of the Right Path,
for by hearing this sutra, they analyze and discern it for the sake of others.
The Buddha again addressed the youth:

"To the north of here, at a distance three times greater than the previous analogy, beyond sixty infinite hundreds of thousands of koṭis of buddha-fields, there is a world named Vyavasthita-ratnajāla. There dwells a Buddha named Candraprabhā-viśuddha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat, who currently teaches the Dharma."

If sons of good family or daughters of good family who study the Bodhisattva vehicle hear the name of that Buddha and believe and rejoice in it without doubt, honoring and delighting in what has been proclaimed by the Eye of the Path, they shall, in every place where they are born, always attain the Ratnaketu Samādhi. They shall behold the Buddha-lands of ten Ganges-sands in each of the ten directions, and they shall transcend hundreds of thousands of billions of koṭis of births and deaths. Established in their initial practice, they shall swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment as the Most Perfectly Awakened One.

If there are women who hear the name of that Buddha and, harboring no doubt, place their trust in my words, they shall, in whatever place they are born, transform their female bodies and obtain male forms; they shall then exhort and convert countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, leading them to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Understanding their sounds and voices, they shall attain non-retrogression and swiftly achieve perfect enlightenment; they shall then expound the scriptures for all beings, leading them to the Great Way of the three vehicles: the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"If one hears the name of the Two-footed One, Their heart becomes joyful and free from hesitation;
They can then cast off unrighteous anxieties, And practice correctly for as many eons as there are rivers."
So too shall it be for those who behold the various Buddhas, serving and making offerings to them beyond measure.
Throughout a single lifetime, with boundless and inexhaustible resources, they provide the most exquisite requisites for worship;
those who are thus able to practice and cultivate the honored path of the Buddha are truly extraordinary.
If there are those who praise the sagely sages with clarity, And upon hearing this, never harbor doubt;
If there are women who hear these names of the Buddhas Without hesitation,
they shall swiftly transform their female bodies And become men whose light shines everywhere.

His radiance shines everywhere without exception; he travels to immeasurable Buddha-lands and beholds all the deeds performed by the multitudes in the world, thereafter attaining Buddhahood and remaining forever free from sorrow.
If one can hear the names of the Buddhas, their power of spiritual travel transcends such as this;
the noble assembly of Tathāgatas is like great dragons—how much more so for those who resolve their minds to seek the Buddha-way!
Reverently honoring the Perfectly Awakened One who is free from defilement, if one hears his name, one should quickly proclaim it;
his radiance shines like the light of the sun, bringing forth the samādhi of meditative concentration and skillful elucidation.
If one can follow and practice this honored path of the Buddha, its extraordinary virtues will be just as described.
Sentient beings are immeasurable and inconceivable; the noble ones exhort them toward the honored path of the Buddha.
Just as the wondrous and majestic lunar palace dwells in the void, manifesting all its radiance, so too are the majestic power and the various marks of one who can uphold the name of the Tathāgata.
Those who have heard the name of the Buddha yet harbor doubts and hesitations—
if they can practice this Dharma with utmost sincerity and diligently cultivate the most honored path— [they shall attain liberation].
Always able to diligently practice the unsurpassed truth, such a person shall not encounter disputes or litigation;
by following the Holy Honored One with boundless conduct, as soon as they hear his name, they immediately take refuge.
The Buddha told the youth:

"Below this world, passing beyond the previous metaphor by ninety-nine times, and further transcending that by as many incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *koṭis* of Buddha-fields as there are in ninety-nine [units], there is a world named Honored Banner Lord (*Guhāpati*). Its Buddha is named King of the Sound of the Well-Pacified Moon (*Sukhaśānticandrarāja*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. The sūtras he proclaims are virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end; he walks alone through the three realms and rescues those of the three periods of time, causing them to resolve upon the Great Way, the unsurpassed, right, and true path."

"If sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who study the Bodhisattva vehicle hear the name of that Buddha and do not harbor doubts in their hearts, but believe what has been explained by my Dharma-eye, they shall attain the Samādhi of Universal Radiance in whatever place they are born."

At the time of their death, they will fully behold hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas appearing before them; this shall be so in each of the ten directions. The Buddhas of the ten directions will preach the sūtras for them, and upon hearing them, they will receive and uphold them, cherishing them in their hearts without ever forgetting. By the time they attain the path of Buddhahood, their meritorious virtues will be incalculable, ten times more than hundreds of thousands of millions of billions. They will attain immeasurable, boundless, and unfathomable *samādhis*, never losing their concentration midway until they reach the path of Buddhahood, remaining unobstructed and supported by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.

For those who are at the stage of new learning, they shall transcend the hardships of birth and death for ninety-nine billion times one hundred thousand kalpas; these bodhisattvas will swiftly approach the unsurpassed, right, and true path, not being hindered by the number of kalpas or the cycle of birth and death, just as when the sun shines forth, the world is filled with great brilliance.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having contemplated this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Hearing the supreme name as one wanders through the world, Being a great immortal (ṛṣi) of infinite billions,
Having beheld hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas, One should personally serve this most excellent one."
By being able to make offerings to all Tathāgatas, acting as a virtuous guide to widely transform and enlighten others,
and universally illuminating the three periods of time, one shall thereafter attain Buddhahood, free from sorrow and affliction.
In a single lifetime, they serve countless Honored Ones as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they swiftly attain the samādhi of "Universal Radiance," and thereafter they become Buddhas free from anxiety.

Thus, his awakened mind becomes vast and insatiable; encountering the Dharma Kings who turn the wheel of Dharma, he establishes sentient beings so that the three evil realms no longer exist, extinguishing the fires of birth and death as water douses them.
The Honored One among gods and humans is the field of merit; Among men, he is the guide of Dharma, his virtue supreme.
When people behold him, they harbor joy; They cast off these eight difficulties here.
The wise attain solitude and tranquility; having attained a human body, they are ever intelligent and sagacious.
After wandering through immeasurable lifetimes, they finally encounter a Buddha, who proclaims the name "Abiding in Peace."
Though one may have established hundreds of thousands of vows, upon hearing this Guide of the World,
who has attained peaceful harmony and the great eye of enlightenment, one shall likewise attain the patience of gentleness (kṣānti).
Just as I received the prediction from Dīpaṃkara, seeing the Buddha and scattering flowers upon him, so too does the wise one attain patience;
thus he speaks of the names of billions of Buddhas and their transcendent, extraordinary vows.
When he radiates light at the time of his passing, there are none who do not proclaim his name;
yet only those of external paths and their deceptive arts sit upon such people, obscuring the Way of the Teachings.
Should there be those who hear this sutra being preached, having personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s proclamation,
and who, in future generations, are able to receive and uphold it, and further explain it in detail for others.
The Buddha addressed the youth:

"To the north, passing from here a distance equal to twice as many grains of sand in the Ganges as mentioned in the previous analogy, there is a world named Well-Discriminated. Its Buddha is named Innumerable Vigor and Vow Chief Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One; he currently dwells there, preaching the Dharma."

I proclaim the Way of the Buddha to transform and enlighten the ten directions, so that all may receive its grace through the six supernormal powers and the six perfections; they shall only study as bodhisattvas to ensure the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.

If good men or good women who study the Bodhisattva Vehicle hear the name of that Buddha, they will harbor no entangling nets of affliction and will believe in my Dharma-eye, remaining ever diligent throughout their successive births.

He does not practice desire; he does not long for his parents; he is not attached to his wife, children, brothers, or sisters; he does not covet his relatives or those of his maternal and paternal lineages; nor does he crave his friends, acquaintances, or associates. Throughout all his successive lives, wherever he may be, his body is never separated from the adornment of the thirty-two marks. With little lust, anger, or delusion, his body is free from disease. He has few anxieties and possesses immeasurable peace and security. Until he attains Buddhahood, he constantly acquires merits and virtues beyond measure, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"I have never seen such grief and sorrow as that of parents and kinsmen;
yet those who hear the names of the Buddhas do not harbor doubt or fetters."
His world is brilliantly radiant; currently residing in the zenith, his majestic spiritual power illuminates the three realms as he expounds the Dharma for the sake of the multitudes.
If one can hear his name and proclaim it to others, [one shall attain liberation].
With the thirty-two marks, he constantly adorns his body;
his wisdom is never diminished as he practices the bodhisattva path.
He reveres and takes refuge in all Buddhas, which is brought about by proclaiming their names.
Wherever they may be, they always revere and honor inconceivable billions of Buddhas;
those who practice the Buddha-way are never attached to anything.
The merits and virtues they have attained can never be fully extolled.
Because they have heard this name, they are able to explain it to others.
Then, in a future age, if they should encounter this title, let them harbor no doubt: the Buddha’s wisdom is the unsurpassed canopy.
Having seen the Equal Enlightenment and made offerings to countless Buddhas,
this sutra will later come into the hands of those who possess the Jewel Net; such Bodhisattvas shall be free from fear.
Having just heard this sutra, do not harbor any hesitation;
do not doubt the Buddha-way, for the Tathāgata is beyond limitation.
In previous lives, you have already practiced it, cultivating it for countless billions of kalpas.
Having bestowed their own bodies, hands, and feet, ears, noses, heads, and eyes, as well as their wives,
children, kingdoms, villages, and cities, they gave these gifts without harboring resentment;
thereafter, in a future life, they shall be those who hear this sutra.
One who is able to explain this to others becomes the supreme benefactor of the multitude.
Those who wish to understand the definitive meaning— the conduct of all Buddhas—
should not harbor hesitation regarding the instructions of the World-Protector.
Therefore, having heard this sutra, one should discipline the mind and practice contentment;
recite and study this scripture, frequently practicing walking meditation,
constantly preaching with diligence, and remaining so for a full three months.
He attained the resolve of dhāraṇī and skillfully maintained mindfulness of all dharmas.

Thereupon, the youth Ratnajāla, having heard the meaning of the True Dharma proclaimed by the Buddha, felt great joy in his heart and offered to the Tathāgata a robe woven with golden threads, its value being beyond measure.

The Tathāgata immediately entered the *samādhi* known as "Just-as-it-is" (*yathāvadbhāva*). From every single pore of the Buddha’s body, he emitted rays of light that illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds in the eastern direction.
All those Buddha-lands in the east clearly beheld this Buddha-field; likewise, the assemblies gathered at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) there also all beheld this Buddha-realm.
At that time, nine hundred and ninety billion trillion members of the fourfold assembly each beheld the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The Buddha addressed the youth Ratnajāla:
"You have now seen the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the inconceivable, incalculable, and boundless worlds to the east of here—vast and exceedingly numerous beyond all analogy."
The youth replied, “I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told the youth:

"For example, the individual names of all the devas and humans in the trichiliocosm could be established through incalculable efforts; yet the names of those Buddhas exceed even that, being beyond measure or record—some are named Śrī (Auspiciousness), and others likewise Suśānta (Well-Quiescent);
some are named Candranirghoṣa (Moon-Sound), and others likewise Candramandala (Moon-Pavilion)."
Some are named Pure, and their flower-radiance is likewise;
some have names such as Transcending the King of Supernatural Powers, and as with one name, so it is for all their various names.
He replied, “I have seen them,
O God among Gods!”
“In the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, it is likewise so, just as you have now seen the number of Buddhas, O Venerable One! Furthermore,
you have been a wheel-turning monarch that many times.”
At that time, the youth Ratnajāla was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and a virtuous mind arose within him.
Then the earth shook greatly, and all sentient beings attained peace and security. That great radiance shone everywhere, exhorting them to cultivate the roots of virtue.
Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of trillions of celestial hosts dwelt in the void, scattering flowers and burning incense as offerings to the Tathāgata.

Śakra and Brahmā, along with their respective retinues, and immeasurable trillions of other devas followed in attendance, raining down red sandalwood, blue lotuses, water lilies, and yellow and white lotuses. Some devas hung down and scattered countless jeweled necklaces. Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of trillions of people from the world came of their own accord to cast themselves at the Buddha’s feet; moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy, tears flowed down their faces. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they recalled the events of countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of trillions of past lives, and beheld from afar the boundless, immeasurable transformations of his supernormal powers.
Thereupon, the devas and humans praised him in verse:
"In incalculable billions, The various devas are everywhere present;
With soft and wondrous fragrant flowers, They scatter them down upon the World-Light."
A hundred million Śakras, lords of the devas, all dwelling together in the midst of space,
offered purple-gold flowers to the Honored One with Two Feet.
A hundred billion Brahmā deities held red sandalwood in their hands.
With scattered rays of light shining forth, they raised their voices in exclamation and praise.
Countless celestial instruments played spontaneously above;
the words they produced were noble and sublime, manifesting stainless radiance.
The gods have hundreds of thousands of lotuses, dwelling in the void to praise the Teacher;
with various flowers and celestial fragrant canopies, they form billions of banners and streamers for the Honored One among Men.
Each held hundreds of thousands of precious necklaces, scattering bright moon pearls as they offered praise to the Buddha;
with hearts full of joy, they made offerings to the Most Honored One, who is supreme, peerless, and of immeasurable majesty.
Hundreds of billions of people, endowed with all virtues, take refuge in the Most Victorious One who is immeasurable;
bowing their heads to the ground, they take refuge, their consciousness of hundreds of millions of eons being beyond all comparison.
At that time, the Light of the World strikes the drum of the Dharma;
responding to the moment, he proclaims it to them, and his fame resounds through billions of lands.
Immeasurable and beyond reckoning, a multitude of billions of people gathers.
The Buddha established him as the most honored and wise among men.
With supreme, wondrous, and solid jewels, and with sandalwood unsurpassed, that natural throne was prepared;
the youth felt a surge of joy within his breast.
Majestic and subtle is this jewel; I receive and uphold the jeweled net.
Manifesting in countless thousands of forms, I offer it to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
With single-minded contemplation, Its value exceeds that of a thousand worlds.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light emanate from the moon-pearls;
with a single mind, all are thus. The precious net radiates majestic brilliance, and the light it illuminates pervades the entirety of Vaiśālī.
With these I offer worship to the World-Protector, the Holy and Wise Lord;
thirty-six thousand precious canopies are presented to the Honored One with Two Feet.
Within these various kinds of precious canopies, the physical forms of all Buddhas appear.
Formed of purple-gold color, as round as a nyagrodha tree;
this supreme precious parasol offered [to the Buddha] has pearls hanging all around it,
and of these precious parasols, there are twenty-five thousand in total.
Thus he made offerings to the World-Honored One, completing them all in an instant.
With golden garments, he bestowed gifts upon the bodhisattvas;
adorning the Buddha-way, they were fully and universally provided.
Twenty-five thousand people, and hundreds of thousands of millions of beings;
multitudes of bodhisattvas numbering in the hundreds of millions, beyond all calculation.
Countless billions and trillions—such is the number they bear.
All come from the eastern direction; so it is with the south and the west.
From the north, the zenith, and the nadir, and likewise from the four intermediate corners—all worlds throughout space are clearly seen by his eyes from afar.
The World-Protectors, the Sovereigns of Sages, possess the hue of purple-polished gold;
the World-Honored One abides therein, radiating brilliant and majestic light.
The various classes of Bodhisattvas have each come from their respective native lands.
The youth Ratnajāla made offerings to this scholar at that time of assembly; his reverence was beyond measure.
The World-Honored One encouraged and comforted him—the supreme among men, the lion of the world.
Toward all devas, nāgas, and spirits, and toward people of high station,
they now stand before the Buddha with single-minded reverence;
as it was in past ages, so too have they made offerings like the sands of the Ganges.
Those who hear this Buddha-sūtra, And practice the conduct of the youth Ratnajālin,
Shall attain the samādhi of right concentration And never regress until they reach Buddhahood.
The merit and reward they obtain Cannot be measured or limited.
For those who uphold this sutra, no comparison can be made for their merit.
One might still be able to know the number of Buddha-lands in the ten directions;
one could even fully comprehend the limits of the elements of water, fire, and wind, and the extent of the earth.
If one upholds this sutra, even if one were to sigh in praise and speak of its limits,
one could not fully exhaustively fathom the measure of its merit and the extent of its virtues.
This applies to bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as laymen and laywomen of pure faith.
The devas and mahoragas who hear this sutra—
when all sentient beings assemble before them, they cannot praise their virtue enough;
their vital essence is not diminished, and even fire becomes cool when they enter it.
For seven days, focus your mind exclusively on this, Practicing the path of the Buddha and making offerings to the Bodhisattvas; One should honor the sutras in this manner.
Should one wish to grasp a thousand worlds With but a single hair’s tip, [it can be done].
Holding it in the palm of one's hand, Not setting it down for billions of kalpas; If,
in the final age of the future, One extensively expounds such a sūtra as this to others,
One will swiftly achieve the path of the Honored One’s awakening.
To be able to explain this to others is truly unprecedented.
The Buddha-way is boundless, and its analogies are difficult to enumerate exhaustively;
yet, in the final age of the future, there will be those of external paths and heterodox studies.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s lion’s roar, they will surely engage in mutual dispute and contention.
Those who revere and honor the Buddha, the Protector of the World who radiates light,
shall hear this sutra with profound humility and respect in the future age to come.
The Buddha told the youth:
"Suppose there were beings of the three grades within a buddha-field who, with one accord and a single mind, were intent upon the wisdom of the Buddha.

Furthermore, suppose someone were to make offerings to them for incalculable kalpas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, presenting these offerings to the Buddha with a single-minded devotion free from duality; and suppose they were to construct a vihāra that is exceedingly vast, as large as a great trichiliocosm, composed entirely of celestial sandalwood."

Within a single monastery, he constructed lecture halls numbering in the hundreds of millions; in each lecture hall, he provided hundreds of thousands of millions of couches, and upon every bed, he spread layers of fine, soft garments.
With ten billion pieces of purple-polished gold as beds and couches, they cause great, holy sages to dwell in the world and make offerings to them with these beds and couches.

After those Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa at the end of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they erect for each and every Buddha a stūpa and temple, as incalculable as the sands of the rivers;
the stūpas and temples erected for each and every Buddha are composed of the seven treasures, as vast as a trichiliocosm, towering so high that they reach the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above.

Upon each and every stupa and temple, there were parasols for offering as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; billions of strings of pearls hung down upon their four sides, and billions of silk banners and upright pennants were likewise as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all adorned with various jewels while the sounds of musical instruments resounded.
